coredata.dc:title: Flexible and wet stable starch films crosslinked with sugar-based aldehydes
coredata.dc:creator: Mu, Bingnan
Xu, Lan
Yang, Yiqi
coredata.dc:description: Starch films always suffer from brittleness and poor wet stability. Besides, numerous reinforcements have enormous limitations. Because of the high reactivity, sugar aldehydes should have substantially improved properties of starch products. However, sugar-aldehydes not only had limited property improvement of starch products but also contained a significant amount of formaldehyde. Various saccharides were oxidized under different conditions to evaluate the generation of formaldehyde and crosslinking performance. Mechanical properties of starch films were controlled by length and concentrations of crosslinkages from formyl-saccharides. Via engineering crosslinkages of formyl-saccharides, tensile strength and breaking elongation of starch films were improved from 7 MPa and 5%–25 MPa and 28 %, respectively. Formyl-saccharide crosslinkages also ensured 93 % weight retention of starch film in water and unchanged cytocompatibility. Less than 2% of crosslinkages formed by formyl-saccharides were damaged at 50 °C for 7 days at various pHs. This work demonstrates that starch films with desirable tensile strength, flexibility, wet stability and cytocompatibility can be developed via structure-controlled formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharide crosslinkages.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Starch films always suffer from brittleness and poor wet stability. Besides, numerous reinforcements have enormous limitations. Because of the high reactivity, sugar aldehydes should have substantially improved properties of starch products. However, sugar-aldehydes not only had limited property improvement of starch products but also contained a significant amount of formaldehyde. Various saccharides were oxidized under different conditions to evaluate the generation of formaldehyde and crosslinking performance. Mechanical properties of starch films were controlled by length and concentrations of crosslinkages from formyl-saccharides. Via engineering crosslinkages of formyl-saccharides, tensile strength and breaking elongation of starch films were improved from 7 MPa and 5%–25 MPa and 28 %, respectively. Formyl-saccharide crosslinkages also ensured 93 % weight retention of starch film in water and unchanged cytocompatibility. Less than 2% of crosslinkages formed by formyl-saccharides were damaged at 50 °C for 7 days at various pHs. This work demonstrates that starch films with desirable tensile strength, flexibility, wet stability and cytocompatibility can be developed via structure-controlled formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharide crosslinkages.

ce:section.ce:para: Synthetic polymer packaging materials have a wide range of superior properties such as toughness, flame-retardant, thermal insulation, corrosion resistance and lightweight. In the last decades, growth of population and industrial productivity led to a sharp increase in the production of synthetic polymers (Mu and Yang, 2022; Sivan, 2011). However, these non-degradable polymer materials are causing severe environmental problems (Mierzwa-Hersztek et al., 2019). Development of biobased polymer materials from polysaccharides, proteins and lipids with desirable properties to replace synthetic polymer materials has substantial potential to solve environmental and health problems of synthetic polymers (Ilangovan et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Mu et al., 2020). Among polysaccharides, starch is a great candidate for coating materials due to its low costs and ideal chemical structures (Sakkara et al., 2020; Şen et al., 2017).

Although tremendous progress has been made, starch materials still face many limitations, such as low mechanical properties and wet stabilities (Niranjana Prabhu and Prashantha, 2018). Adding nanoparticles plasticization and chemical crosslinking are common approaches to improving the mechanical properties of starch films (Cheng et al., 2021; do Lago et al., 2021; Ojogbo et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). However, in most cases, nanoparticles further lowered the flexibility of starch films and plasticizers, which always were added 30 % more based on weight of starch, lowered the tensile strength and water stability of starch products (Guna et al., 2019; Haq et al., 2019; Tabasum et al., 2019). Crosslinking without delicate design always had limited improvement in strength and elongation of starch films and need high quantities of plasticizers. A summary of the mechanical properties of starch with various reinforcements is included in the Results and Discussion.

Among crosslinkers, biobased crosslinkers are popular because of their safety, biocompatibility and sustainability. Citric acid is a common crosslinker extensively used in carbohydrates, proteins and other biobased products (Reddy and Yang, 2010; Xu et al., 2017). Starch films crosslinked with citric acid had substantial improvement in breaking strength and wet stability. However, flexibility of starch films was not improved with citric crosslinking. Limited flexibility improvement resulted from high crosslinking temperature citric acid required and limited crosslinkage length citric acid provided. High crosslinking temperatures up to 170 °C, remarkably damaged starch molecules, thereby reducing the properties of starch. Short crosslinkages limited slippage between starch molecules. As a result, the breaking elongation of starch films was poor.

To improve the flexibility of starch products, starch crosslinking required mild reaction conditions and controllable crosslinkage lengths. Mild reaction conditions minimize damages to starch molecules. Controllable length of crosslinkages promote starch molecules slippage with each other and improve the flexibility of starch products. Formyl-saccharides were proven to substantially improve breaking elongations of amine-rich biobased materials such as chitosan and protein. (Mi et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2022). Among pure starch products, formyl-saccharide-crosslinked starch films should have top mechanical properties and water stabilities. Compared to previous publications, such starch films should be suitable for various applications such as food packaging and coatings (Thakur et al., 2019). However, due to the lack of design and control of structure of formyl-saccharides, crosslinking performance is still not satisfactory (Liu et al., 2015). For example, sugar-aldehyde-crosslinked starch films were still brittle and need excessive plasticizers, more than 20 % based on the weight of starch, to increase the flexibility of starch films (Xu et al., 2015). Furthermore, we found that a significant amount of formaldehyde contained in sugar aldehydes developed by previous work was generated. Toxic formaldehyde interfered the crosslinking performance with sugar aldehydes. As a result, the actual crosslinking performance of sugar-aldehydes was difficult to be measured. Finally, the application range of formyl-saccharides is narrow.

This work employed chemical crosslinking to improve the interactions between starch molecules and mobilities of starch molecules simultaneously. Improvement of interactions between starch molecules and mobility of starch molecules contribute to the improvement in tensile strength and breaking elongation of starch films, respectively, and are controlled by crosslinking degrees and length of crosslinkages. Crosslinking degrees can be adjusted by concentrations of crosslinkers and length of crosslinkages can be adjusted by saccharide oxidation conditions. Other critical properties like stability of crosslinkages and cytocompatibility were investigated. The work hypothesizes that starch films with desirable wet stability, flexibility, strength and cytocompatibility can be developed via the establishment of structure-controlled formyl-saccharide crosslinkages. Via the use of formyl-saccharides as a high-efficiency crosslinking agent, the application scope of starch can be widened remarkably.

The procedures were adopted from the previous work and modified for generation of formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharides (Xu et al., 2015). Series of formyl-saccharides with different amount of aldehydes and length between aldehydes were developed. For sucrose-based crosslinkers SU1, SU2 and SU3, 5 g of sucrose was reacted with 3.1 g, 6.2 g and 9.3 g of sodium periodate, respectively, for 5 h at room temperature in water. For raffinose-based crosslinker RA4, 5 g of raffinose was reacted with 8.5 g of sodium periodate for 5 h at room temperature in water. The pH of reaction medium was kept at 5.5 ± 0.1. Reacted oxidant was precipitated via addition of barium dichloride into reaction medium followed by filtration to obtain solution of formyl-saccharides. In addition to SU1, SU2 and SU3, different molar ratios of periodate to raffinose (RA3, RA4 and RA5) were also tried. Four crosslinkers that could provide four different lengths of crosslinkages were reported. Since RA3 had a similar length of crosslinkages as SU2 and RA5 had a similar length of crosslinkages as RA4, only SU1, SU2, SU3 and RA4 were reported.

Sample solutions of formyl-saccharides were divided into parts for determination of oxidation level and molecular mass, respectively. For determination of oxidized sugar ring, formyl-saccharide solution was hydrolyzed in 3 M HCl overnight at 60 °C to break all glycosidic bonds. The condition was adopted from a previous work (de Wit et al., 1989). After the hydrolysis, formyl-saccharides in solutions were derivatized with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to increase resolutions in HPLC (Honda and Kakehi, 1978). For determination of molecular mass of formyl-saccharides, samples were directly derivatized with 2,4- dinitrophenylhydrazine to convert all aldehyde groups to Schiff base. For the HPLC analysis, a C-18 reversed-phase column (Acclaim 120, 120 Å, 4.6 × 250 mm, 5 μm) and a UV–vis detector were equipped in the HPLC system. The samples (25 μL) were injected and eluted at a flow rate of 1 ml/min at 30 °C. A mixture of solvents water-acetonitrile (55:45 v/v) was used as the mobile phase. The UV–vis detector was set at 360 nm. Molecular weight was measured using an HPLC-MS (Thermo Scientific MSQ Plus, Electrospray ionization mode with positive polarity at a probe temperature of 350 °C and a cone voltage of 60). The detector was set to scan the range of 200–2000 m/z.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of length of formyl-saccharide crosslinkages
ce:section.ce:para: The structures obtained from HPLC-MS were optimized using Gaussian 09 package. Structures of formyl-saccharides were optimized via DFT calculations till the total energy of the structures reached the lowest level. After the optimization, crosslinkage length of formyl-saccharides was obtained by measuring distances between aldehyde groups. We used B3LYP functions under DFT calculation since B3LYP is generally faster than most functions and yields comparable results. It is also fairly robust and not heavily parameterized. 6-31G + g(d,p) was used as a basis set to properly describe chemical bonds and long-range interactions such as dispersion and hydrogen bonds.

Generally, 3 wt % of starch with 5 wt% of glycerol based on weight of starch was added into distilled water to prepare 50 g solution, which was heated at 90 °C for 30 min till a homogenous solution was formed. For crosslinking films, 0.3∼3 g of crosslinker solution containing 5 wt% formyl-saccharides were added to the starch solution. Glycerol converted hemiacetal linkages, formed after reactions between aldehydes on formyl-saccharides and hydroxyl groups on starch, to acetal linkages. As a result, the stability of crosslinked starch films is strengthened. Starch films were peeled from the plates 96 h after solution casting. Then films were treated at 150 °C for 5 min. After heating, the films were conditioned at 21 °C and 65 % relative humidity.

Tensile properties of films were determined on an MTS tensile tester (Eden Prairie, MN) with a 500 N load cell according to ASTM Standard D 882−02. The average thickness of films was between 0.15 to 0.20 mm.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of water stability of films
ce:section.ce:para: Starch films were incubated in distilled water at room temperature and 50 °C for different time followed by calculation of weight retention of films.

The growth state of NIH3T3 cell assessed the cytocompatibility of starch films with and without formyl-saccharide crosslinking. Samples were sterilized at 120 °C for 60 min before cell culture. The cells were incubated onto the samples and cultured at 37 °C for 3 days. Then, the samples were washed with PBS, and placed in a 24-well plate. The dyeing buffer contained 10 μL Calcein-AM and 10 μL PI-DNA in 10 mL. Subsequently, the NIH3T3 cells cultured on samples were observed under a fluorescent microscope (Leica DMI8, Buffalo Grove, IL). The optical density of the liquid was determined at 490 nm using a fluorescent microscope.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Measuring the molecular weight of polysaccharides
ce:section.ce:para:
Viscosity average molecular weight of starch was measured via converting intrinsic viscosity (η) to molecular weight of starch using Mark-Houwink relation. The intrinsic viscosity of starch was obtained from relative viscosity (ηr) and specific viscosity(ηsp), which were acquired using a Ubbelohde viscometer, and concentration of polysaccharides (C) based on the relationship that η = (ηsp/C)C→0 = (ln ηr/C)C→0. Since molecular weight of starch could be obtained via well documented Mark-Houwink equation specified for starch, a reference starch was not needed. The molecular weights of starch film with and without crosslinking were determined in a solution of 90 % DMSO/H2O based on a Mark-Houwink relation, adopted from Merle et al’s work, as shown in Eq. (1) (Millard et al., 1997).
(1) [η] = 1.2DPv 0.3

ce:section.ce:section-title: Retention of crosslinkages between aldehydes and hydroxyl groups at different pHs
ce:section.ce:para: Glycerol and formyl-oligosaccharide were reacted at 150 °C for 5 min with the ratio of glycerol to aldehydes 1.5:1. The reactants were derivatized with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to calculated unreacted aldehydes via measuring amount of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine using HPLC. Then reactants were under heat at 50 °C for 7 days with different pH before derivatized with 2,4- dinitrophenylhydrazine to calculated hydrolyzed acetal bonds.

The approach based on a simplified methodology (Zeng et al., 2021) was adopted. Each of the uncrosslinked and crosslinked starch films was mounted flat onto the inner wall of a cuvette and measured using a Beckman Coulter DU 720 UV–vis spectrophotometer. The opacity of the film was obtained via Eq. (2).
(2) Opacity = A/x
Where A is the absorbance of a film at 600 nm and x is the thickness of a film (mm). The wavelength was selected because it is commonly used for the opacity measurement of starch films.

Prior to color measurement, starch films were conditioned at 21 °C and 65 % relative humidity for at least 72 h. Color difference, ΔE (CIELab), between crosslinked and uncrosslinked films, and CIE whiteness index of films were determined using an X-Rite Ci7800 spectrophotometer (X-Rite, MI, USA). D65 was used as the illuminant with a 10 ° observer. The diameter of the port plate aperture was 25 mm. Each sample was measured 3 times and the mean from the measurements was reported.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Development of formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharides with different lengths of crosslinkages
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 1 shows conditions for developing formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharides. The pH control, molar ratios of periodate to saccharides, and reaction time were crucial for developing formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharides. The sugar-aldehydes developed by the previous research contained (1:3 of molar ratio of periodate to saccharides without pH control for more than 24 h) a substantial amount of formaldehyde, preventing the large-scale applications of sugar-aldehydes as crosslinkers (Xu et al., 2015). In addition to the toxicity of formaldehyde, it also interferes with the crosslinking performance of formyl-saccharides. With control of pH and reaction time, formaldehyde-free formyl-saccharides were developed to crosslink starch.

Table 1 shows the series of formyl-saccharide crosslinkers with different aldehyde amounts and lengths between aldehydes. Results show that varying molar ratios of saccharides and sodium periodate can control aldehyde amount and length between aldehydes on formyl-saccharides. For example, with molar ratio of sucrose to periodate 1:1, aldehydes mainly on fructose ring of sucrose. Though aldehyde amounts and lengths between aldehydes on major crosslinker structures from SU1 and SU2 were similar, 12 % of SU2 was sucrose-tetraaldehydes, the major structure of SU3. As a result, the crosslinking performance between SU1 and SU2 might be different. According to DFT calculations (Density functional theory), the lengths between aldehydes are from 2 to 15 A.

Based on Table 2 , crosslinking using formyl-saccharides did not whiteness of starch films based on statistical analysis. The highest color difference, indicated by ΔE (CIELab), between crosslinked and uncrosslinked starch films was 0.67, indicating that formyl-saccharides crosslinking led to minimal or slight color differences. Opacity of starch films was slightly changed by crosslinking. The thickness of films had no significant differences between uncrosslinked and crosslinked films. The results agree with most research that crosslinking did not remarkably change thickness, color and opacity of biobased products (Versino et al., 2016).

Fig. 2 demonstrates improvement of strength and flexibility of starch films reinforced by formyl-saccharides with different lengths of crosslinkages and degrees of crosslinking. Fig. 2a and b show with the same aldehyde amounts in starch films, SU1 had the least crosslinking performance followed by SU2 because SU1 had the least increase in molecular weight of starch, as shown in Fig. 2b. SU3 and RA4 had similar crosslinking performance since both crosslinkers increased the similar degrees of molecular weight of starch. A low degree of crosslinking performance resulted in limited improvement of mechanical properties of starch films. For example, the tensile strengths of SU1 and SU2 crosslinked films were 8.32 ± 0.9 and 12.12 ± 2.11 MPa, respectively and breaking elongations of SU1 and SU3 crosslinked films were 5.03 ± 0.09 % and 7.1 ± 1%, respectively. The low crosslinking performance of SU1 and SU2 could be attributed to the short length between aldehydes, which were unlikely to form plenty of intermolecular crosslinkages. The increase in length between aldehydes substantially raises the chance to form intermolecular crosslinkages. However, with similar degrees of crosslinking, crosslinkage length determined mechanical properties. Formyl-saccharides with long length of crosslinkage preferably increased breaking elongation of starch films and moderately short crosslinkage length preferably increased the breaking strength. To correlate mechanical properties to degrees of crosslinkings, a low concentration of crosslinkers was used because a low degree of crosslinked starch was soluble and measurable for molecular weight. Results show that though a similar increase in molecular weight of starch, films crosslinked with RA4 had a better elongation, while films crosslinked with SU3 had a better breaking strength. The tensile strength of films crosslinked with SU3 and RA4 were 18.97 ± 1.07 MPa and 7.9 ± 0.8 MPa, respectively. The breaking elongation of films crosslinked with SU3 and RA4 were 9 ± 0.05 % and 15.24 ± 0.1 %, respectively. The main difference between SU3 and RA4 was the length between aldehydes. The long distance between aldehydes contributed to the long length of crosslinkages, promoted slippage of the molecular chains of starch, and eventually increased breaking elongations rather than the breaking stress. Since brittleness is the major drawback of starch products, RA4 was chosen as the crosslinker because it substantially improved starch flexibility. Fig. 2c shows the effect of concentrations of RA4 on the improvement of flexibility of starch films. Finally, breaking elongation of starch films was increased by up to 540 %. A decrease in elongation and tensile strength of films was observed when crosslinkers were higher than 0.7 mmol/g because concentrations of crosslinkers higher than 0.7 mmol/g will substantially increase the rigidity and decrease flexibility of starch molecules. As a result, the mobility of starch molecules was restricted. When exerted with external forces, the stress could not be distributed evenly among starch molecules and slippage between starch molecules was difficult. Therefore, both tensile strength and elongation were lowered. The FTIR results in Fig. 2d show that majority of crosslinkers reacted with hydroxyl groups on C-6 of starch. Compared to uncrosslinked starch, a new peak at 1080 cm−1 emerged in crosslinked starch. The peak at 1080 cm−1 was due to the stretching vibration of CO bonds formed between crosslinkers and hydroxyl groups on C6 of starch. Since hydroxyl groups on C6 of starch have less steric hinderance compared to hydroxyl groups on C2 and C3 of starch, crosslinkers are likely to react with hydroxyl groups on C6 of starch.

Fig. 3 further shows effects of crosslinkers with different crosslinkage length on morphologies of starch polymer and final mechanical properties. Interactions between intermolecular hydrogen bonds dominate mechanical properties of starch products (Chen et al., 2004). Intermolecular crosslinkages affect cleavages and restoration of intermolecular hydrogen bonds in starch. Weak points always exist in starch molecules. External forces always first break hydrogen bonds in weak points so that starch molecules separate and starch products crack. Intermolecular crosslinkages could strength those weak points in starch materials via strengthening interactions between starch molecules. Fig. 3a illustrates the morphology of starch molecules with crosslinker SU3, which provided relatively short crosslinkages. Starch molecule backbones could be stretched by external forces till the emergence of a new weak point. After such a stretch, the overall alignment of starch molecules improves. As a result, breaking stress of starch films substantially increased as well as the breaking elongation and Young’s modulus, as shown in Fig. 3b and c. Fig. 3a also illustrates how crosslinker RA4 substantially improves the flexibility of starch films. Long crosslinkages brought by RA4 have a limited effect on strengthening interactions between starch molecules but could help increasing starch backbone length and thus promote slippage between polymers. Therefore, starch molecules could further be rearranged. As a result, the breaking elongation of starch films also improved greatly. Slippage between starch molecules would gradually increase the interactions between starch molecules and result in a “straining hardening” segment in stress-strain curve of RA4 crosslinked starch film, as shown in Fig. 3b. Specific properties of starch films can be improved by adjusting the structures of crosslinkers. For example, designing formyl-saccharides with short lengths between aldehyde groups helps improve the breaking strength, while designing lengthy crosslinkages helps reduce the brittleness of starch films. Fig. 3d quantifies the relationship between crosslinkage length from formyl-saccharides and mechanical properties of starch films. Results agree with the mechanism illustrated in Fig. 3a. The breaking strength of starch film increased linearly with the increase in crosslinkage length when the length was less than 5 Å. When the crosslinkages were longer than 5 Å, little improvement of breaking strength was observed. The reason is that long crosslinkages had limited effect on strengthening the interactions between starch molecules. For breaking elongation, an increase in length of crosslinkages always linearly increased the breaking elongation of starch films because long crosslinkages help increasing length of starch backbones and slippage between starch molecules. When the crosslinkage length was less than 5 A, crosslinkages had a larger improvement of tensile strength than breaking elongation.

Fig. 4 a shows starch films had substantial improvement of wet stability after being treated with formyl-saccharides. With the same concentration of aldehydes in starch films, SU3 and RA4 crosslinked starch films had better wet stability than SU1 and SU2 crosslinked films because SU3 and RA4 had a higher chance to form intermolecular crosslinkages in starch polymers. Starch films with formyl-saccharide crosslinkage also had good wet-stability at high temperatures such as 50 °C. SU3 crosslinked starch films had better wet stability than RA4 crosslinked because starch molecules crosslinked with SU3 had stronger molecular interactions.

Fig. 4b shows weight retentions of SU3 crosslinked starch films after being immersed in water for different days. The results show that weight retention decreased to 93 % when films were immersed in water for 10 days. The weight retention kept unchanged when films were immersed in water for more than 10 days. Results show that formyl-saccharide-crosslinked starch films had not only good flexibility but also desirable wet stability.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Stability of acetal crosslinkages of formyl-saccharides
ce:section.ce:para: Formyl-saccharide-crosslinkages in starch films were stable. To quantify the stability of acetal crosslinkages in starch products, a simulation reaction between formyl-saccharides and glycerol was conducted. Table 3 shows the stability of acetals between formyl-saccharide and hydroxyl groups. Glycerol was used to test stability of acetal crosslinkages for the following reasons. First, we used glycerol to transform hemiacetal formed between formyl-saccharides and starch to acetal. Second, the structure of glycerol is simple and similar to monomers of starch. Also, previous works used glycerol as the model compound to study the crosslinking of polysaccharides (Yao et al., 2013). Since aldehyde groups on SU3 and RA4 had similar chemical properties, SU3 was used to study the stability of crosslinkages. Results show that acetals were stable between pHs 5–9 at 50 °C for at least seven days. The results indicate that crosslinked starch films are durable for daily use.

Fig. 5 shows that formyl-saccharides did not change the cytocompatibility of starch films with NIH3T3 cells. As shown in Fig. 5, the relative viability of NIH3Ts cells on films with and without formyl-saccharides crosslinking was the same. Results demonstrate that starch films reinforced with formyl-saccharides have wide-scale applications, including food coating, because of the non-toxicity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison in properties of starch materials from previous work
ce:section.ce:para: Compared to commercial petroleum-based films, starch films always had much lower mechanical properties. However, among pure starch products, formyl-saccharide-crosslinked starch films had top mechanical properties and water stabilities. Compared to results from previous work, starch films developed by this work should be suitable for various applications such as food packaging and coatings. Addition of nanoparticles and plasticizers, and chemical crosslinking are common approaches to improving the mechanical properties of starch films. However, in most works, nanoparticles further lowered the flexibility of starch films and plasticizers, which always were added 30 % more based on weight of starch, lowered the tensile strength and water stability of starch products. Crosslinking always had limited improvement in strength and elongation of starch films and need high quantities of plasticizers. Table 4 compares starch films reinforced by various approaches. Those starch films which had similar improvement or absolute values of elongation and tensile strength as formyl-saccharide-crosslinked starch films were incorporated with other polymers equivalent to 100 % weight of starch, such as chitosan and carboxymethyl cellulose as well as 30 % plasticizers based on weight of starch. The starch in this work only used 5% of formyl-saccharides as crosslinker and 5% glycerol as a plasticizer and crosslinking stabilizer.

Formyl-saccharides were developed to improve array of properties of starch products. With fine control of crosslinkages, 5% formyl-saccharide and 5% glycerol provided the top mechanical properties of films among starch products. Crosslinker SU3, which provided moderately short length of crosslinkage, preferably helped improve the tensile strength of starch while crosslinker RA4, which provided moderately long length of crosslinkages, preferably improved the flexibility of starch. Finally, after crosslinking, wet stable starch films had a 540 % increase in flexibility and a 400 % increase in breaking strength. Fine crosslinking design ensured 93 % weight retention of starch in water at room temperature and unchanged cytocompatibility. Crosslinkages formed by formyl-saccharides were stable in the conditions for daily uses.
